newsitem.title: USA: Fierce battle develops for Republican Party chair.
newsitem.headline: Fierce battle develops for Republican Party chair.

text.p: A fierce battle that is developing for the post of Republican Party chairman is beginning to expose ideological differences within the party.

At least seven candidates have thrown their hats into the ring to succeed Haley Barbour, who is retiring as party chairman after four highly successful years in the job during which the party gained control of both houses of Congress in 1994 and retained it this year.

The contest for chairman will be decided by 165 members of the Republican National Committee -- three from each state, the District of Columbia and four U.S. territories -- when they meet in Washington Jan. 17. A simple majority of 83 committee votes is needed for election.

Officials of the Christian Coalition, a powerful conservative faction within the party, were quoted last week as saying they controlled 35-40 votes on the committee and would insist on a candidate acceptable to them.
All but one of the candidates are members of the committee. The sole outsider is retiring New Hampshire Gov. Steve Merrill, who was an active member of Bob Dole's unsuccessful presidential campaign.

Among other leading candidates is David Norcross of New Jersey, who has the backing of delegates from the Northeast as well as New Jersey Gov. Christine Whitman. But Norcross supports limited abortion rights, which may rule him out in the eyes of conservatives.
The Republican Party in general is more and more dominated by Southerners, who may want to pick one of their own as chairman. Barbour is from Mississippi.

California Republican chairman John Herrington and Colorado chairman Jim Nicholson would also likely be acceptable to conservatives. The only woman in the contest is former Florida state chairman Jeanie Austin, who believes Republicans must do a better job of reaching out to women.

President Clinton outpolled Dole by 16 percentage points among women in last month's presidential election and Austin told Reuters that was because many women saw the Republican Party as "mean-spirited and intolerant."
"I'm very conservative. But I accept that the Republican Party is a big tent and we need to bring more people in, not drive them away," she said.

The latest candidate to announce seems likely to be Texas Republican state chairman Tom Pauken, an ultra-conservative who is close to the Christian Coalition as well as Pat Buchanan, the right-wing columnist who ran second to Dole in the contest for the Republican presidential nomination.

Republican sources said Pauken would formally announce his candidacy either Wednesday or Thursday. But some Republicans fear Pauken would be too divisive as party chairman and would drive away moderates and women voters.
